entries.note: He is summarising his own piece, so he endorses it. Neither 'no AI SaaS story' nor 'everything rides on selling GPUs' has one reading that most readers would test the same way.
This is hyperbole about OpenAI's funding needs. Taken literally it is not a serious claim.

entries.test: Public reporting or company disclosures on whether millions of NVIDIA GPUs that have been sold remain uninstalled or not powered on.
entries.note: This is a compound claim. 'Endless debt' is rhetorical and 'no longer makes sense to buy' is normative, so only the claim about uninstalled GPUs is graded.

entries.test: OpenAI's reported or disclosed cumulative 2025 revenue through the end of September 2025, compared with around $4.5 billion.
entries.note: 'Vast difference' is his own characterisation. The figure he compares against is the $4.3 billion first-half figure reported by other outlets.

entries.test: Whether revenue from AI products and services ever reaches the cumulative cost of the NVIDIA GPUs bought for AI.
entries.note: This is an open-ended 'never' forecast. Only clear evidence that payback happened could settle it.

entries.test: OpenAI's cash, revenue and funding compared with its scheduled Oracle payments, and Oracle's built data-center capacity compared with what the $300 billion contract requires.
entries.note: In practice this is about whether the deal could be carried out in future years. Later payment and delivery events would also bear on it.

entries.test: The sum of OpenAI's announced compute and data-center commitments due within roughly four years of September 2025, compared with $1 trillion.
entries.note: 'Pull any of it off' is ambiguous between doing any of the deals and doing all of them; the proposition keeps his wording.
He states it as a firm 'expectation'; the proposition softens it to 'likely'. Whether people 'act like AI is the most special thing' until they accept otherwise has no shared test.
